newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Crompton targets utility firms.
newsitem.headline: India's Crompton targets utility firms.

text.p: Indian electrical engineering firm Crompton Greaves Ltd said on Tuesday it was zeroing in on the country's state-run electricity boards as buyers for a new energy efficient transformer it will launch in a year's time.

Crompton Greaves has tied up with U.S. engineered materials maker Allied Signal International Inc, to jointly develop amorphous metal transformers of large KVA ratings for both export and domestic markets, company officials said.
"We have already made a few prototypes," said Ranjan Dasgupta, president of the firm's Power Systems division.
"Within six months to eight months we'll start supplying them to customers."

Dasgupta said the medium-size transformers, made by Crompton Greaves with material supplied by Allied Signals, would cut core power losses by upto 80 percent, as compared to conventional transformers.
"It will really take off in the next two years," he said.
Crompton Greaves is looking at transformers with ratings of 500 KVA and above, which Dasgupta said were best suited for power utilities in urban areas as well as hospitals and cinemas.
"India's distribution sector uses around 150,000 transformers annually," said G.L. Dua, a power consultant with Allied Signals. "About 10 percent of that market falls within this category."
Dua estimated there was a market of about one to two billion rupees annually for the amorphous metal type of transformer.
"It's a question of a choice between imported energy inefficient materials and imported energy-efficient material," Dua said, adding that India imports all its transformer core material at present.
"Firms like BSES, and Ahmedabad Electricity Co Ltd have already asked for prototypes," Dasgupta said. "We are manufacturing five or ten units in the 500 KVA and 1,000 KVA categories."

A number of state-run firms like the Bombay Electric Supply and Transport Undertaking (BEST), the Delhi Electricity Supply Undertaking (DESU), the Calcutta Electric Supply Company had also shown interest, Dasgupta said.
India's loss-making utilities were not in a position to pay for new equipment, Dasgupta said, but he did not expect the situation to continue very long. "The scenario has to change," he said.
He expected 50 percent of the amorphous metal transformer production to be exported within two years, he added. Possible destinations would be Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand, he said.
"Our current orderbook for transformers is in excess of four billion rupees," he said. "50 percent of them are for export."
Dasgupta said Crompton Greaves' results last year had not been good, and he expected '97/98 to be identical to '96/97, "if not worse".
"But we have already blocked the power systems orderbook with export orders," he added. "76 percent of the capacity at our Kanjurmarg plant has been booked with export orders."
Britain's BTR Plc, a diversified conglomerate, has a 16 percent stake in Crompton Greaves.
